title: Power Personalization and Indoctrination in Dictatorships
text:
## Power Personalization and Indoctrination in Dictatorships

##### Katerina Tertytchnaya a, Wooseok Kim b, Anja Neundorf b, Ksenia Northmore-Ball c, and Eugenia Nazrullaeva d

| aUniversity | of Oxford |
| --- | --- |
| bUniversity | of Glasgow |
| cQueen Mary, | London |
| dUniversity | of Konstanz |

Abstract Conflict over the distribution of power within a leadership group is central to authoritarian politics, and contemporary autocracies show increasing concentration of authority in individual leaders. Yet we know comparatively little about how the personalization of power shapes strategies of information control through education and the media. We combine new cross national data on indoctrination with indicators of power personalization across 212 authoritarian regimes from 1950 to 2010. We find that as leaders personalize power, they not only centralize control over education and the media, but also systematically politicize their content, expanding investments in political and patriotic indoctrination. These findings extend research on the consequences of power personalization, demonstrating that it systematically influences strategies of political control beyond repression.

### 1 Indoctrination

Conflict over the distribution of power within a leadership group is a central feature of authoritarian 
politics (e.g., Geddes et al., 2018, 92). Across personalist, military, and single-party regimes, leaders 
regularly attempt to concentrate authority in their own hands. As shown in Figure 1, levels of power 
personalization have steadily increased across authoritarian regimes since the 1960s, reflecting a 
global shift toward more leader-centered rule. This trend has renewed scholarly interest in how 
power personalization affects governance and political control (e.g., Colgan and Weeks, 2015; 
Kendall-Taylor et al., 2017; Morgenbesser, 2018; Frantz et al., 2020; Bonvecchi and Simison, 2015; 
Chin et al., 2023). 
Existing research shows that as leaders consolidate power at the expense of other elites, they 
increasingly rely on repression to eliminate challengers and deter opposition (e.g., Frantz et al., 
2020; Davenport, 2007a). A related body of work links intra-elite power dynamics to leaders’ 
efforts to control educational, media, and cultural institutions, showing that as power becomes more 
personalized, leaders face diminishing pressures to maintain media openness as a commitment 
device to reassure coalition partners (e.g., Sheen et al., 2022; Beiser-McGrath, 2024). In parallel, rich 
single-country studies, such as those on Stalin, Mao, and Ben Ali, as well as work on totalitarianism 
document how highly personalized rule often coincides with personality cults, leader-centered 
education, and regime-serving national identities (e.g., Brandenberger, 2012; Sanina, 2017; Arendt, 
1951; Linz, 2000). What remains unclear, however, is whether these patterns are idiosyncratic to 
particular leaders and historical moments or whether they reflect a systematic relationship between 
power personalization and indoctrination across regimes. At the same time, comparative research 
on education and media control has focused primarily on institutional centralization rather than 
the politicization of substantive content. This focus is understandable given the historical lack of 
systematic cross-national measures of indoctrinating content, but it obscures an important distinction: 
the centralization of education or the media alone does not necessarily imply indoctrination. Leaders 
may take over media outlets to reward loyalists or centralize education for developmental or efficiency 
reasons (Paglayan, 2022).

We build on research linking power-sharing arrangements to autocrats’ strategies of political 
control by examining how the personalization of power shapes efforts to mold citizens’ beliefs 
through education and the media. Moving beyond existing work that focuses on leaders’ control 
over these institutions, we assess whether the content they produce becomes more politicized as 
personalization deepens. Our theoretical contribution lies in showing that personalization heightens 
leaders’ capacity and incentives not only to centralize control over media and education systems 
but also to shape the substantive messages citizens encounter. Empirically, we leverage new 
cross-national data that, for the first time, allow us to evaluate whether personalization is associated 
with shifts in the political and patriotic content of educational curricula and media outputs across 
a global sample of autocracies. By distinguishing institutional control from the politicization of 
messages, our analysis provides the first comparative evidence on how personalization affects the 
content of information citizens receive in a comparative setting. 
We distinguish between two interrelated pathways through which power personalization shapes 
indoctrination. First, personalization strengthens leaders’ incentives and ability to centralize control 
over educational and media institutions. When power is more dispersed, leaders often tolerate media 

openness as a commitment device to reassure coalition partners and maintain transparency (e.g., 
Sheen et al., 2022; Beiser-McGrath, 2024). As authority becomes concentrated in a single leader, 
these constraints diminish: veto players who might resist centralization are sidelined, and actors 
such as media owners, bureaucratic elites, and regional officials lose the leverage needed to block 
expanding state control over education and communication. Second, leaders can use control over 
these institutions to shape content that promotes political and ideological narratives to legitimize 
their rule, foster loyalty, or signal dominance. 
Although these two pathways describe how personalization enables indoctrination, we also 
recognize that personalization and indoctrination can reinforce each other over time. As leaders 
sideline rival elites, they gain greater discretion to politicize education and the media; these narratives 
can, in turn, weaken rivals by reducing their popular support and legitimacy. This feedback dynamic 
does not undermine the expectation that personalization precedes expanded indoctrination, but it 
helps explain why higher levels of personalization are systematically associated with greater use of 
indoctrination. 
Using a measure of personalism proposed by Geddes et al. (2018) and leveraging original 
cross-national data on the use of indoctrination in educational settings and the media from 1945 
onward (Neundorf et al., 2023), we find that the process of power personalization is associated with 
not only increased state control of education and the media but also with growing investments in 
political education and patriotism. We complement the quantitative analysis with an in-depth study 
of Russia. This allows us to illustrate some of the steps through which the personalization of power 
is associated with increased investments in indoctrination. 
Our work responds to recent calls in the study of authoritarianism to move beyond a predominant 
focus on repression and to examine non-violent strategies of political control (e.g., Przeworski, 2022; 
Hassan et al., 2022). We advance understanding of indoctrination as a strategy of societal control 
in regimes where power becomes increasingly concentrated in the hands of a single leader. Our 
findings suggest that the personalization of power shapes strategies of information control directed 
at ordinary citizens. This is an important contribution to the literature. Existing cross-sectional 

time-series analyses of personalization have largely focused on how dictators secure elite loyalty, paying considerably less attention to how they use information control to manage citizens’ beliefs and behaviors. Building on research from single case studies, our paper develops a theoretical argument about the relationship between personalism and indoctrination and tests this connection using rich cross-sectional time-series data. Findings suggest that information control is a systematic feature of power personalization, not an idiosyncratic strategy limited to a few well-studied regimes. Altogether, our results broaden understanding of the consequences of personalization, demonstrating that investments in information control and indoctrination are central to the consolidation of personalized rule.

### 2 Personalism and strategies of political control

Typologies of authoritarian regimes disagree on how best to classify ‘personalism,’ or the concentra tion of power and policy-making authority in the hands of a single individual. For example, in an earlier work, Geddes (1999) defined personalist regimes as a standalone category, distinguished from single-party regimes and military dictatorships by the concentration of power in the hands of the leader. Although personalist regimes are often supported by political parties or by the military, they are not restricted by these organizations (e.g., Geddes, 2003, 52). For other scholars, such as Brooker (2013) or Hadenius and Teorell (2007), personalism is a ‘secondary’ or ‘supplementary’ feature of a regime or a “continuous trait that may be more or less present” across regimes but also within a single regime over time (Hadenius and Teorell, 2007, 145). We side with this latter line of research. Our concept of power ‘personalization’ captures the over time shifts in the balance of power between a leader and his elite.1 Over time, an individual leader may emerge and concentrate more power

1What makes personalization different from autocratization is increasing focus on a single individual, “unrivaled in terms of personal power, policy influence, and control” (Baturo and Elkink, 2021). We also distinguish power personalization from regime consolidation, which Merkel (1998) describes as a long-term process through which institutions, elites, and citizens come to accept the regime as the only legitimate order. Personalization and consolidation can move independently or even in opposite directions.

than other elites, whether in personalist dictatorships or single-party and military regimes (see, also Frantz et al., 2020). Personalization emerges from leaders’ efforts to renegotiate power-sharing arrangements within the ruling coalition (Svolik, 2012). However, as elites are marginalized and veto players removed, this transformation also reshapes how rulers approach the broader problem of political control. Following Hassan et al. (2022, 157), we define political (or societal) control as “any tactic through which the state seeks to gain compliance from society.” Concentrated power allows leaders to move beyond managing elites toward managing the masses, investing in strategies that sustain mass compliance once intra-elite conflict has been resolved. Authoritarian leaders pursue political control through a range of strategies. Some rely on violent repression, which forces citizens to comply with state directives and suppresses the opposition’s ability and willingness to challenge the

regime.2

Strategies of political control also include tactics of information control. To communicate regime principles to the broader population through the media, autocrats can also take over media outlets, stifle critical voices, and dictate news production and coverage to emphasize the regime’s legitimizing narratives. Propaganda, censorship, and indoctrination, a deliberate and intentional “regime-led socialization process” (Neundorf et al., 2024, 4), delivered through schools, media, mass organizations, the workplace, and the arts can ensure that citizens comply with state directives (e.g., Wolf, 2023; Belodubrovskaya, 2017; Esberg, 2020).
